extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, Wittgenstein scholars, graduate students in philosophy/mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Wittgenstein's middle and later views on mathematics, especially his critiques of set theory, the nature of irrational numbers, finitism, decidability, and the role of extra-mathematical application. Intended to clarify the development and key theses of Wittgenstein's philosophy of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrational numbers as rules, not infinite extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrational numbers should be understood as rules for constructing finite expansions (an 'unlimited technique of expansion'), not as completed infinite mathematical extensions or infinite series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgenstein insists that 'the concepts of infinite decimals in mathematical propositions are not concepts of series, but of the unlimited technique of expansion of series' (RFM V, §19). Treating irrational numbers as completed infinite entities engenders pseudo-concepts and foundational mistakes; e.g., remarks such as 'the further expansion of an irrational number is a further expansion of mathematics' illustrate the danger. Use finitistic descriptions and avoid reifying infinite expansions as extensional objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain intension–extension distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conflate intensions (laws, rules, descriptions) with extensions (lists, enumerations); the one is not a substitute for the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgenstein repeatedly warns that treating laws and enumerations as essentially the same leads to error (PG 461; PR §180). Examples: you cannot legitimately infer from having a description that you thereby have an enumeration; Dedekind's treatment of infinite classes misapplies a 'description' as if it were an extensional test. Preserve a categorical difference when analyzing mathematical concepts and avoid substituting intensional descriptions for extensional verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fictitious infinite symbolism; mathematics uses actual finite signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is concerned only with the signs with which it actually operates; one must avoid presupposing an actual infinite symbolism of signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set theory's 'fictitious symbolism' (PR §174; PG 469) leads to nonsense when one assumes mathematics can represent the actual infinite. The proper approach focuses on what can be symbolically operated upon in practice (finite signs and rules), not on positing infinite sign-objects or pictorial infinities that do not enter the calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor diagonal proves non-enumerability (relative), not greater cardinality
rubrics_metrics.description: Cantor's diagonal construction shows that for any given definite real-number concept / recursive enumeration one can construct a number not in that enumeration (non-enumerability), but it does not establish that one infinite 'set' is greater in cardinality than another (non-denumerability as a cardinality claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgenstein distinguishes non-enumerability (failure of a particular kind of recursive enumeration) from claims that one infinite multiplicity is 'greater' than another (RFM II, §§1,10,22,29). The diagonal yields a new real relative to the stipulated concept; it does not prove the existence of completed infinite extensions of differing cardinalities. Beware moving from 'not recursively enumerable' to 'greater cardinality'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical meaningfulness requires an applicable decision procedure (algorithmic decidability)
rubrics_metrics.description: An expression counts as a meaningful mathematical proposition within a calculus only if we knowingly have in hand an applicable and effective decision procedure by which we can decide it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgenstein treats undecidable or non-algorithmically-decidable expressions (e.g., the unrestricted statement 'There are three consecutive 7s in the decimal expansion of π') as not genuine mathematical propositions unless finitistically restricted or rendered decidable (RFM V, §9; LFM 31–32). The distinction between 'provable in principle' and 'proved / decidable by an applicable procedure' is crucial: the latter grounds mathematical meaningfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics is human invention (anti-Platonism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is our invention; mathematical entities and calculi do not pre-exist as discoverable objects—mathematicians invent calculi rather than discover pre-existing mathematical facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgenstein denies Platonist pictures of pre-existing mathematical worlds and warns that seeing mathematics as a 'natural history of numbers' is misleading (RFM I, §168; RFM IV, §11). This criterion advises against treating mathematical possibility or provability as ontological facts independent of human practices and rule-inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finitistic constructivism: interpret 'infinite' as unlimited technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Where 'infinite' appears in mathematics, prefer reading it as indicating an unlimited technique or rule (a mode of generation) rather than a completed infinite extension or cardinal magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgenstein emphasizes that expressions like 'there are infinitely many even numbers' point to a limitless method/rule for generating numbers, not to a gigantic completed extension (RFM V, §§14,19; LFM 31). Avoid treating symbols like ℵ0 as cardinals attached to actual infinite extensions; instead analyze the differing techniques involved in learning/using numerals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra-mathematical application as necessary for mathematical status
rubrics_metrics.description: For a sign-game or formal calculus to count as mathematics it must have uses outside pure formalism; extra-mathematical application (use in practices beyond mathematics) is a necessary condition of being a mathematical language-game.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Later Wittgenstein reintroduces this demarcation: 'it is essential to mathematics that its signs are also employed in mufti' (RFM V, §2). If a formal system lacks anchoring in extra-mathematical practice, it is merely a sign-game or mathematical architecture that 'hangs in the air' (RFM II, §35). Use this test to distinguish meaningful mathematical activity from purely formal manipulations (e.g., critique of set theory's lack of application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics consists of calculi (syntactical operations), not propositions-as-ontological-facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical activity should be understood as operating within calculi—rule-governed, syntactic transformations—rather than as statements that correspond to mathematical facts existing independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgenstein: 'Mathematics consists of [calculi | calculations], not of propositions' and stresses that proofs 'make new connexions' rather than reveal pre-existing ontological relations (MS 121; RFM III, §31). Emphasize rule-following, transformations, and the constructive/invented nature of proofs when evaluating mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decidability changes the status of a question when an applicable procedure is invented
rubrics_metrics.description: When a question becomes decidable—i.e., when an applicable decision procedure is known or invented—its status as a mathematical proposition changes; a new 'connection' is thereby made in the calculus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgenstein notes that a question or proposition 'becomes' decidable and that inventing a decision procedure creates a new connexion that did not previously exist (RFM V, §9). This supports evaluating mathematical claims in light of the available procedures rather than positing their decidability in principle without procedural grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reify provability or modal possibility as mathematical actuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid treating 'provable in principle' or modal claims about possible proofs as if they are actual mathematical facts; provability-in-principle is not identical to being proved or having an existing connection in the calculus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgenstein criticizes the modal reification that equates possibility with actuality (RFM I, §21; PR §§141,144). Claims that a proof 'must exist' or that the possibility of a proof is a mathematical reality are misleading. Evaluate mathematics by what is proved or what procedures are in hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate among systems of irrational points; no exhaustive system of all irrationals
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize there are many diverse systems ('systems of irrational points') each given by recursive rules, but there is no single exhaustive system or 'set of all irrational numbers' as a higher-order infinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgenstein: Cantor shows many diverse systems of irrational numbers, but we cannot construct an exhaustive system of all irrationals (RFM II, §§29,33). Interpret claims about 'the real numbers' cautiously, restricting to definite recursive concepts when asserting enumerability or completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess interest and meaning by anchoring to practice and application
rubrics_metrics.description: If a calculus or theory lacks anchoring in extra-mathematical practice, its propositions may be uninteresting or merely rhetorical; meaningfulness and interest are measured by practical anchoring and application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgenstein suggests subjecting the interest of calculations to a test of their application; without extra-mathematical anchoring (e.g., set theory's foundational claims), propositions like 2^{ℵ0} > ℵ0 become architectural and unanchored (RFM II, §62; II, §35). Use the presence or absence of application as an evaluative criterion for the significance of mathematical theories.
